why.text: The reader decides how much each passage counts through attention, and the gate works by scaling it.
Every result is reported as the share of questions whose predicted answer matches exactly.

spans.text: A question-answering system first fetches passages that might hold the answer, then reads them. Until now the reader treated every fetched passage as equally trustworthy, so a few irrelevant ones could drown out the one that mattered.
This paper adds a small gate that scores each passage against the question first, so the reader listens mostly to the passages that look relevant.

items.text: A retriever fetches candidate passages for the question.
The gate gives each passage a score between 0 and 1 from the question and the passage together.
The reader weights its attention to each passage by that score, then writes the answer.

spans.text: Exact match rose by 2.1 points on Natural Questions and 3.4 on HotpotQA compared with FiD-base, the strongest reader it was tested against.

analogy.text: Like an editor who skims a pile of clippings and marks the relevant ones before the writer starts: the writer still reads everything, but pays most attention to what was marked.
Where it breaks: the editor can only mark clippings that are in the pile — if the retriever missed the right passage, the gate cannot bring it back.

plain.text: Put the question and passage i side by side, turn them into one relevance number with learned weights, and squash that number into a score between 0 and 1.
